news_title: GAO reports cyber threat problems at FDA and USDA
efet_title: GAO reports cyber threat problems at FDA and USDA
efet_body:
The Government Accountability Office has found that the FDA and USDA are not properly prepared to share information on cyberattack threats in real time.
Auditors also found that the Food and Drug Administration had not met a requirement to develop plans for responding to food-related cyber emergencies.

Wolverine Packing Co. Recalls Ground Beef Products Due to Possible E. Coli O157:H7 Contamination
Wolverine Packing Co.
Quantity Recovered
22,755 lbs
FSIS Announcement
WASHINGTON, Nov. 20, 2024
– Wolverine Packing Co., a Detroit, Mich. establishment, is recalling approximately 167,277 pounds of ground beef products that may be contaminated with
E. coli
O157:H7, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) announced today.
The fresh products have a “use by” date of 11/14/2024 and the frozen products are labeled with production date 10 22 24.
View full product list
.
View labels
.
The products subject to recall bear establishment number “EST. 2574B” inside the USDA mark of inspection. These items were shipped to restaurant locations nationwide.
The problem was discovered when FSIS was notified by the Minnesota Department of Agriculture of a group of ill persons who had reported that they consumed ground beef prior to their illness.
FSIS was notified of illnesses on November 13, 2024, and working in conjunction with Minnesota Departments of Agriculture and Health, FSIS determined that there was a link between the ground beef products from Wolverine Packing Co. and this illness cluster. On November 20, 2024, a ground beef sample collected by the Minnesota Department of Agriculture as part of an outbreak investigation tested positive for
E. coli
O157. To date, 15 case-patients have been identified in one state with illness onset dates ranging from November 2, 2024, to November 10, 2024. FSIS continues to work with the Minnesota Departments of Agriculture and Health on this investigation.
Anyone concerned about an illness should contact a healthcare provider.
E
. coli
O157:H7 is a potentially deadly bacterium that can cause dehydration, bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps 2–8 days (3–4 days, on average) after exposure the organism. While most people recover within a week, some develop a type of kidney failure called hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). This condition can occur among persons of any age but is most common in children under 5-years old and older adults. It is marked by easy bruising, pallor, and decreased urine output. Persons who experience these symptoms should seek emergency medical care immediately.
FSIS is concerned that some product may be in restaurant refrigerators or freezers. Restaurants are urged not to serve these products. These products should be thrown away or returned to the place of purchase.
FSIS routinely conducts recall effectiveness checks to verify recalling firms notify their
customers of the recall and that steps are taken to make certain that the product is no longer available to consumers.
FSIS advises all consumers to safely prepare their raw meat products, including fresh and frozen, and only consume ground beef that has been cooked to a temperature of 160 F. The only way to confirm that ground beef is cooked to a temperature high enough to kill harmful bacteria is to use a food thermometer that measures internal temperature,
https://www.fsis.usda.gov/safetempchart
.
Consumers and members of the media with questions about the recall can contact Don Tanner, company representative at 248-762-1533.

efet_title: E. coli infections documented at Tufts University - Food Safety News
efet_body:
An outbreak of E. coli infections among students at Tufts University is under investigation.
As of Nov. 19 there were five confirmed cases, according to the university health services. The infections are suspected to have stemmed from Fresh at Carmichael Dining Center, according to Tufts Daily.
The Medford Board of Health inspected Carmichael on Nov. 18 but found no evidence to suggest the dining hall should be closed, according to an email sent to students. Officials from the board will return on Nov. 21 as the situation continues to be monitored. There is also no evidence that other Tufts dining facilities have been affected.
“As part of the investigation, public health officials are interviewing affected individuals, reviewing menus, and looking into food suppliers,” the email read. “Tufts is cooperating fully with the Medford Board of Health and the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, including providing information about ingredients, purchasing, suppliers, and products served as requested to support the ongoing investigation.”
Tufts reported in 2022 that the Carmichael Dining Center feeds 1,000 to 1,700 students a day. Carmichael
closed in early September
after a water leak from a room above the kitchen affected the hall’s HVAC, electrical and plumbing systems, Tufts Daily reported at the time.

WASHINGTON, May 24, 2026 -
The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) is issuing a public health alert due to concerns that beef kofta products served at The Kebab Shop restaurant locations may be contaminated with Shiga toxin-producing
E. coli
(STEC) O157:H7. A recall was not requested because the products are no longer available for purchase.
The beef kofta was produced as a raw ground beef product by Olympia Food Industries, Inc. dba Olympia Foods (Est. 18743) in Franklin Park, Illinois, on January 6, 2026, and supplied to The Kebab Shop restaurant locations in California, Texas, and Florida.
The problem was discovered as part of an ongoing illness outbreak investigation. FSIS, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH), and local health departments in California are investigating a localized outbreak of
E. coli
O157:H7 that includes 9 sick people in California. As of May 24, 2026, illness onset dates have been reported ranging from March 27, 2026, to April 30, 2026. Because the identified illnesses are limited to California, CDPH is leading this investigation with FSIS. FSIS continues to keep its federal partners informed as the investigation progresses. FSIS collected raw ground beef kofta product samples that tested positive for
E. coli
O157:H7. Further testing is ongoing to determine if the product samples are related to the specific outbreak strain.
FSIS is issuing this public health alert to ensure that consumers in California, Texas, and Florida are aware of the outbreak. The Kebab Shop stopped selling beef kofta at all of its restaurant locations on May 18, 2026.

O157:H7 is a potentially deadly bacterium that can cause dehydration, bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps 2 to 8 days (3 to 4 days, on average) after exposure to the organism. This condition can occur among persons of any age but is most common in children under 5 years old and older adults. It is marked by easy bruising, pallor, and decreased urine output. Consumers who ate beef kofta from any location of The Kebab Shop and develop symptoms of STEC infection within 10 days of exposure should contact their health care provider. news_title: Thieves steal $30,000 worth of meat from tractor-trailer in Northeast Philadelphia while driver sleeps - CBS News
efet_title: Thieves steal $30,000 worth of meat from tractor-trailer in Northeast Philadelphia while driver sleeps - CBS News
efet_body:
At least a dozen boxes of meat valued at $30,000 were stolen from the back of a tractor-trailer Thursday morning in Northeast Philadelphia, police said.
The theft happened just after 4:15 a.m. at 11620 Caroline Road. The tractor-trailer, which had Iowa license plates, was hauling meat from Swift Meats, headquartered in Greeley, Colorado.
The driver parked outside a local wholesale distributor around 2 a.m. for a scheduled delivery and fell asleep, police said. They woke to movement in the trailer and saw two masked men in black removing boxes of meat from it.
A dark-colored minivan and a dark-colored sedan were parked behind the trailer.
The driver honked the horn to scare the suspects, but they continued removing the boxes. The driver called 911, and the suspects fled shortly after, police said.
When officers arrived, they discovered that the trailer's lock had been cut and about 3 1/2 pallets of meat, valued at $30,000, were stolen, police said.
Around 4:45 a.m., an off-duty SEPTA police officer spotted stacked boxes of meat on the road at Richmond and East Pacific streets in the city's Port Richmond neighborhood, about 14 miles from where the theft occurred.
CBS News Philadelphia was there as police helped load at least a dozen of the recovered boxes back into the tractor-trailer.
The boxes contained various meats, including one that contained more than 65 pounds of boneless beef chuck eye.
No arrests were made.
This is the latest meat-related theft in a recent uptick in meat heists reported across the city. These thefts often involve entire pallets of meat worth tens of thousands of dollars.
Last month, masked thieves made off with about
$40,000 worth of beef
while the driver slept.
The theft is still under investigation.

news_title: Sierra Nevada Graziers Raw Cheese E. coli Outbreak Ends - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_title: Sierra Nevada Graziers Raw Cheese E. coli Outbreak Ends - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_body:
The Sierra Nevada Graziers raw cheese E. coli outbreak has ended with 18 sick in 10 states, according to the
CDC
. That is an increase of five more patients and one more state since the last update was issued in September 2026. The new state is New Mexico.
The case count by state is: California (6), Colorado (1), Georgia (2), Kentucky (1), Michigan (1), New Mexico (1), Nevada (3), Oregon (1), Tennessee (1), and Utah (1). The patient age range is from one to 58 years, with a median age of four. Illness onset dates range from July 7, 2026 to September 20, 2026. Nine patients in this outbreak have been hospitalized. Three of them have developed hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a type of kidney failure that is common in E. coli patients who are five years old and younger.
Epidemiological data showed that Sierra Nevada Cheese Company Graziers raw milk cheese was contaminated with E. coli O26 bacteria and made people sick. All of the company’s cheeses were
recalled
.
Whole genome sequencing showed that bacteria from patient samples are closely related genetically, which means that people in this outbreak likely got sick from eating the same food. In addition, 100% of 15 patients who were interviewed reported eating Sierra Nevada Graziers raw milk cheese. That percentage is significantly higher than the 4.9% of people who ate unpasteurized cheese in the FoodNet Population Survey over the same time period.
Officials in California collected leftover Graziers raw milk cheese from a sick person’s home for testing. Whole genome sequencing showed that the cheese was contaminated with the same strain of E. coli O26 as the patients in this outbreak. In addition, the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development collected an open sample of the cheese from a consumer’s home. Testing by the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services showed that it tested positive for a different strain of E. coli.

news_title: Case Count in Ohio University’s E. coli Outbreak Increases to 17 - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_title: Case Count in Ohio University’s E. coli Outbreak Increases to 17 - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_body:
The case count in the Ohio University’s E. coli outbreak has risen to 17, according to
news reports
. The outbreak is occurring on the Athens campus. This is an increase of six more patients since the outbreak was reported
earlier this month
. The health department says symptoms began November 5 to 10, and WOUB reported on November 18 that one person was hospitalized and has since been released.
All 17 patients got sick at around the same time, which suggests a common source. But the source or sources of the pathogen have not been identified, and the health department can’t say whether there is an ongoing risk of exposure.
In the past, E. coli outbreaks have been linked to
frozen fruit
,
ground beef,
and
onions
. In other words, the pathogen can contaminate almost any type of food. Outbreaks at universities are also not uncommon. In 2023, an E. coli outbreak at the
University of Arkansas
sickened at least 42 people, and in 2022, a small E. coli outbreak at
San Diego State University
sickened two students. This pathogen can also be passed person-to-person, or if an ill employee handles food.
Symptoms
of an E. coli outbreak usually take three to four days to manifest after infection, but sometimes they don’t occur until a week to ten days later. A complication of this infection, hemolytic uremic syndrome (
HUS
), which is a type of kidney failure, can also occur, although that syndrome is much more common in young children and people with chronic health conditions.
If your child is a student at that university and has been ill with those symptoms, encourage them to see a doctor. They may be part of this outbreak.

news_title: FDA final report on Salmonella outbreak traced to japalenos fails to reveal grower, exporter - Food Safety News
efet_title: FDA final report on Salmonella outbreak traced to japalenos fails to reveal grower, exporter - Food Safety News
efet_body:
The FDA has posted an Executive Summary report on an investigation into Salmonella infections traced to jalapeño peppers. The agency continues to refuse to name the supplier or grower of the peppers.
The outbreak was first reported to the Food and Drug Administration on July 10 by its Minneapolis District Emergency Response Coordinator of an emerging cluster of Salmonella Javiana cases with a signal for Chipotle Mexican Grill.
Ultimately the outbreak sickened 488 people across 38 states with 26 of the patients requiring hospitalization. No deaths were reported.
There were likely many more people sickened in the outbreak than were reflected in the official count. This is because some people do not seek medical attention and others are not specifically tested for Salmonella infection. The CDC estimates that for every patient identified in a Salmonella outbreak there are 29 who go undetected.
Initially the outbreak was associated with Chipotle and QDOBA restaurants, but FDA investigators found that jalapeño peppers sold at retail locations were also a source of the Salmonella.
During the initial phase of the investigation and continuing through to its end, the FDA found jalapeño peppers imported by Coast Citrus Distributors of San Diego, CA, to be the outbreak vehicle. The names of the supplier, grower and ranch the peppers were grown on in Sinaloa, Mexico, were redacted in the FDA’s executive summary.
“In addition to issuing three assignments for traceback record collection, between 9/7-9/15/2026, an FDA team conducted an inspection at
(redacted)
. A 483 was issued noting personnel, sanitation, and cross-contamination issues,” the executive summary states.
Between July 27 and Sept. 10, FDA collected two jalapeno pepper retail samples associated with QDOBA and Chipotle locations of interest an environmental sample, and four dead-end ultrafiltration (DEUF) water samples from
(redacted)
.
State officials and Chipotle Mexican Grill HQ also collected retail samples of produce items from Chipotle locations of interest. All samples were negative for Salmonella.
On July 22, Coast Citrus Distributors initiated a limited recall of jalapeno peppers, which was expanded on Aug. 5, to include all remaining jalapeno peppers imported from
(redacted)
.
“On 9/24/2026,
(redacted)
was added to the red list of Import Alert 99-35, detention without physical examination of fresh produce that appears to have been prepared, packed or held under insanitaiy conditions,” according to the executive summary.
“Due to strong epidemiological association and traceback convergence, jalapeno peppers distributed by Coast Citius Distributors, supplied by
(redacted)
and grown by
(redacted) at (redacted)
ranch were confirmed as the outbreak vehicle.”

efet_title: Oysters from Virginia river continue to test positive for Salmonella - Food Safety News
efet_body:
The Virginia Department of Health is reporting that a third round of oysters taken from Little Wicomico Oyster Company cages on Nov. 2 tested positive for Salmonella, representing three of eight meat samples from two of the company’s four leases.
The Little Wicomico River in Northumberland County, VA, remains closed to shellfish harvest with no end date. CDC counts 28 people sick with Salmonella Telelkebir in 13 states, five of them hospitalized and none dead. Recalled oysters were harvested Sept. 18 through Oct. 8 and shipped to 16 states and the District of Columbia.
On Oct. 13, 400 oysters were pulled from the company’s cages and processed into eight meat samples; all eight were positive, carrying Salmonella Telelkebir, Newport, Hartford and Braenderup. On Oct. 21 a second 400-oyster round was positive on three of the four leases, with Telelkebir, Newport, Hartford and Thompson. On Nov. 2 a third round was positive on three of eight samples from two of four leases. A fourth round was collected Nov. 9 and results are pending at the state lab.
The river cannot reopen until three rounds in a row come back clean.
Virginia also looked for where the Salmonella might be coming from. Forty-seven water samples collected Oct. 22 were tested for HF183, a marker of human sewage, and for Enterococci, a general fecal indicator. HF183 was negative in all 47 and Enterococci ran from below the detection limit to 120 MPN per 100 milliliters. The state health department says the data do not point to a significant sewage release.
Eight bird-feces samples collected Nov. 2 were negative for Salmonella. Oysters from the river’s public harvest grounds, sampled Oct. 26, were negative. Water and oysters from the public grounds collected Nov. 4 went to the University of North Carolina and are pending.
The health department closed the river by emergency order on Oct. 9. When that 30-day order ran out, it replaced it with
Shellfish Area Condemnation 010-105
, with no expiration date.
Eleven of the 28 outbreak patients reported eating raw oysters, and tag and traceback records for seven of them led back to the Little Wicomico River. Two of those seven ate oysters from this river only.
FDA’s safety alert
, lists distribution to California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Missouri, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and the District of Columbia, and says the oysters may have been shipped further.
The recall covers shellstock oysters harvested from the Little Wicomico River between Sept. 18 and Oct. 8, tagged Little Wicomico River, VA, or Little Wicomico River Lower, VA. Publix sold some of them as James River Oysters through Oct. 14. If you shucked and froze oyster meat in late September or early October and are not sure where it came from, throw it out.
